champion: Spinal cord compression due to metastatic tumor
ordered_diagnoses: Spinal cord compression due to metastatic tumor

facts.raw_span: A 50-year-old man
no significant past medical history
1-week history of rapidly progressive gait disturbance
no back pain, fevers, night sweats, or weight loss
full strength throughout all extremities
decreased sensation from the T3 dermatome downward
four beats of clonus bilaterally
hyperreflexia in the lower extremities
profound ataxia, rendering him unable to walk more than a few steps
Contrast-enhanced MRI of the thoracic spine demonstrated a diffusely enhancing lesion centered at T1 with near-circumferential epidural extension causing severe cord compression
CT of the thoracic spine showed an expansile bony lesion of the T1 vertebral body with extension into the left pedicle and posterior elements
CT scans of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis revealed no evidence of a primary malignancy

concepts.preferred_label: Spinal cord compression due to metastatic tumor
concepts.why: The patient's rapidly progressive gait disturbance and decreased sensation from the T3 dermatome downward, combined with the imaging findings of a diffusely enhancing lesion centered at T1 with near-circumferential epidural extension causing severe cord compression, suggest spinal cord compression due to a metastatic tumor.

The imaging findings of an expansile bony lesion of the T1 vertebral body with extension into the left pedicle and posterior elements, combined with the absence of evidence of a primary malignancy, suggest a metastatic lesion of the thoracic vertebral body.
The patient's decreased sensation from the T3 dermatome downward, combined with the presence of clonus, hyperreflexia, and ataxia, suggest a spinal cord injury.

The imaging findings of an expansile bony lesion of the T1 vertebral body with extension into the left pedicle and posterior elements, combined with the absence of evidence of a primary malignancy, suggest multiple myeloma as a possible diagnosis.

The imaging findings of a diffusely enhancing lesion centered at T1 with near-circumferential epidural extension causing severe cord compression, combined with the absence of evidence of a primary malignancy, suggest lymphoma as a possible diagnosis.

The patient's rapidly progressive gait disturbance and decreased sensation from the T3 dermatome downward, combined with the imaging findings of a diffusely enhancing lesion centered at T1 with near-circumferential epidural extension causing severe cord compression, suggest a spinal epidural abscess as a possible diagnosis.
The patient's decreased sensation from the T3 dermatome downward, combined with the presence of clonus, hyperreflexia, and ataxia, suggest a spinal cord infarction as a possible diagnosis.

The imaging findings of a diffusely enhancing lesion centered at T1 with near-circumferential epidural extension causing severe cord compression, combined with the absence of evidence of a primary malignancy, suggest a thoracic disc herniation as a possible diagnosis.

rationales.F10: The presence of a diffusely enhancing lesion centered at T1 with near-circumferential epidural extension causing severe cord compression is highly suggestive of spinal cord compression due to metastatic tumor.
rationales.F11: The expansile bony lesion of the T1 vertebral body with extension into the left pedicle and posterior elements is highly suggestive of thoracic vertebral body metastasis.
rationales.F12: The absence of evidence of a primary malignancy on CT scans of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis makes metastatic tumor less likely.
